"How long will your volcano take?" asked Hrithik, who had finished his solar-system mobile days ago.

When I was fifteen, the Class 10 board exams were a week away. I made a beautiful timetable. Saturday: all of history and geography. Sunday: all of science. I coloured it in. I felt so organised.

I ended up studying late for a week. I passed, but not the way I'd hoped.

Dear Pallavi,

Thank you for asking us to redesign your restaurant's menu and signage. You asked if we could finish in two weeks.

I'd love to say yes. But before promising, I looked at our last five similar projects. On average, they took five weeks. The fastest took three. Each one had printing delays and at least one round of changes we didn't expect.

So here is what I'd suggest. I've broken the job into four parts: design ideas (one week), your feedback (one week), final artwork (one week), printing and fitting (one week). I've added a one-week buffer for the unexpected.

That makes five weeks. I know it's longer than you hoped. But I'd rather give you a date I can keep than one I'll miss.

If two weeks is essential, we could do the menu first and signage later.

Warm regards,
Mridul

You asked how I stopped missing deadlines, Samir? I'm Lavanya, and I used to miss every single one.

My old way: someone asked how long, and I'd imagine myself working perfectly, no interruptions, no mistakes. "Three days," I'd say. It always took eight.

Now I do three things.

First, I look back. How long did the last similar report actually take? I keep a little log now, so I know. Usually, about twice what I'd guess.

Second, I break it into pieces. Research, draft, review, fixes. Each piece gets its own time. That shows me parts I forgot.

Third, I add a buffer. Not a huge one. Maybe a third extra.

Then I give a date. My manager was surprised the first time I said "ten days" instead of "three". But I delivered on day nine.

It feels less impressive. But people trust my dates now. That's worth more.

Class teacher's note, Class 11

Ritu told me today she wants to leave school after Class 11 to become a full-time content creator. She showed me three videos of creators who dropped out and now "earn crores". "If they could, so can I. It's easy."

I didn't dismiss her. I asked, "How many people do you think tried the same thing and didn't make it?"

She hadn't thought about it. Those people don't make videos about failing.

We looked together at a small study the school counsellor had shared: of hundreds of young creators who started full time, only a handful earned enough to live on. Most quietly returned to studies or other jobs.

Ritu went quiet. She said, "I only ever see the ones who made it."

I suggested she keep creating on weekends, finish school, and talk to her parents and the counsellor together.

Aparna

In the girls' hostel common room, Madhuri had pinned up a list: "Habits of Billionaires." No breakfast. Four hours' sleep. Read fifty books a year. Never take a day off.

Neelam, her roommate, read it with a frown. "Where did you get this?"

"An article about famous founders. They all do this."

"And the people who do all this and don't become billionaires?"

"...I don't know."

"My brother tried the four-hours-sleep thing. He got sick and failed two papers. Nobody wrote an article about him."

Madhuri paused. She had only read about the winners. She had never seen a single story about someone who followed the list and failed.

"So the list isn't wrong," Neelam said. "It's just missing everyone else."

Madhuri took down the "no breakfast" and "four hours' sleep" lines that evening. She kept "read fifty books."

qa.q: How many hours of sleep were on Madhuri's list?
qa.a: Four hours' sleep.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri think the list would make her successful?
qa.a: Madhuri felt hopeful and inspired, seeing only famous founders with these habits and not the many who did the same and failed.

qa.q: What did Neelam say that helped Madhuri?
qa.a: Neelam asked about the people who follow the list and fail, and shared her brother's story, showing the missing part of the picture.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel when Madhuri took down some lines?
qa.a: Neelam probably felt relieved, especially about the sleep and breakfast lines.

grounding: A student copies a list of founders' habits without seeing the many who had the same habits and failed.

The poster in the Pune office canteen said: "20 of our graduates now work at top tech firms!" Yusuf was sold. "I'm signing up for this coding bootcamp," he told Ishita. "Look at the results."

Ishita, who worked in HR, read the poster twice. "Twenty. Out of how many?"

"Does it matter?"

"It really does. If twenty joined, that's amazing. If two thousand joined, that's one percent."

Yusuf looked it up. The bootcamp didn't say. He emailed them. The reply was vague: "Many hundreds of students."

"And what happened to the rest?" Ishita asked. "Where are the ones who didn't get jobs? Are they on any poster?"

Yusuf sighed. "No."

"I'm not saying don't go," Ishita said. "Just ask to speak to a few random graduates, not the ones on the poster."

He wrote that down.

qa.q: How many graduates did the poster say worked at top firms?
qa.a: 20 of our graduates now work at top tech firms!

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling as she read the poster twice?
qa.a: Ishita felt doubtful and curious, wondering what the whole group looked like before praising the bootcamp.

qa.q: What did Ishita suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Ishita suggested asking how many joined and speaking to random graduates, so the failures become visible before deciding.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel after the vague email reply?
qa.a: Yusuf probably felt disappointed and more cautious, noticing the bootcamp was hiding the full picture.

grounding: A thoughtful HR worker asks how many joined a bootcamp and where the failures are before praising its results.

I'm Manoj, and I run operations at a small logistics firm. Last month my boss wanted to copy a competitor's strategy: cut prices by half for three months to grab customers. "It worked for SpeedMove," he said. "They're huge now."

I asked something that made the room go quiet: "How many companies tried the same thing and went under?"

Nobody knew. So Pranav, our analyst, looked it up over the next week. He found eleven other firms in the region that had tried heavy price cuts in the last five years. Two survived. Nine closed or were sold cheaply.

"We only remember SpeedMove because it survived," Pranav said. "The others aren't around to tell their story."

My boss was annoyed at first. But he looked at the list for a long time.

We didn't copy the strategy. We tested a small discount in one city instead.

qa.q: How many of the eleven other firms survived?
qa.a: Two survived.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when asking the question in the meeting?
qa.a: Manoj seemed cautious and curious, wanting to know about the failures before praising the strategy, even though it made the room go quiet.

qa.q: What did Manoj and Pranav do that led to a better decision?
qa.a: They looked for everyone who tried the strategy, not just the survivor, and then tested a small discount instead of copying it.

qa.q: How might the boss have felt looking at the list?
qa.a: The boss was annoyed at first, then probably thoughtful and a bit relieved to have avoided a risky move.

grounding: A thoughtful worker asks how many firms tried a strategy and failed before praising one survivor's success.

In the village near Gangtok, Dolma had come home for the Losar holidays. At dinner, her uncle said again what he always said: "Old things were better. My grandfather's plough lasted fifty years. The new ones break in five."

Noor, Dolma's college friend visiting from Delhi, nodded politely.

Later, walking by the fields, Noor said, "Your uncle's plough story is interesting."

Dolma laughed. "I used to believe it too. But think: his grandfather probably had many ploughs. Some broke in a year. We only see the one that lasted fifty years because it's still here."

Noor thought. "So the old things that broke are gone. And we compare the one survivor to all the new ones."

"Exactly. Some new ploughs are bad. But the old weak ones aren't around to be counted."

Dolma didn't correct her uncle at dinner. But she smiled when he said it again.

qa.q: How long did the uncle say his grandfather's plough lasted?
qa.a: My grandfather's plough lasted fifty years.

qa.q: What does Dolma feel when her uncle repeats his story?
qa.a: Dolma feels fond and quietly amused, understanding why the story seems true but not needing to correct him.

qa.q: What insight did Dolma share with Noor?
qa.a: Dolma explained that only the surviving old plough is seen, while the old ones that broke are gone, so the comparison is unfair.

qa.q: How might Dolma's uncle feel if she explained this?
qa.a: The uncle might feel a bit challenged or amused, and may still prefer his memories of the old plough.

grounding: A young professional hears that old tools were better made and notes that only the durable ones remain to be seen.

Kaito had moved from Tokyo to work in Hanoi, and on weekends he explored the old quarter with his colleague Bao.

At a café, an old man at the next table said, "Buildings were made properly back then. Look at these colonial houses. A hundred years and still standing. The new towers crack in ten."

Bao nodded. "My grandmother says the same about songs. Old songs were all beautiful."

Kaito smiled. "But we only hear the old songs that people kept singing. The bad ones were forgotten long ago."

Bao thought. "And the buildings?"

"The weak houses from a hundred years ago collapsed or were torn down. We only see the strong ones."

"So we compare the best of the old to all of the new."

"Right. Some new towers are badly built. But the old weak ones aren't here to compare."

Bao laughed. "Don't tell my grandmother. She'll never forgive you."

qa.q: How long did the old man say the colonial houses had stood?
qa.a: A hundred years and still standing.

qa.q: What was Kaito feeling when the old man spoke?
qa.a: Kaito felt curious and a little amused, noticing that only the surviving old buildings and songs remain to be seen.

qa.q: What did Kaito's point about old songs help Bao see?
qa.a: It showed that people remember only the good old songs, just as only the strong old buildings remain, so comparisons with the new are unfair.

qa.q: How might Bao's grandmother feel hearing Kaito's view?
qa.a: Bao's grandmother might feel offended at first, since she loves the old songs and sees them as better.

grounding: A young professional abroad hears that old buildings were better made and notes that only the durable ones remain.

But Shankar had the green one. And Imtiaz. And the twins. They played together every evening by the gate. When I brought my wooden top, they laughed.

Class teacher's note, December

This term, a fidget-spinner craze swept Class 4. By the end of November, almost every child had one.

Yusuf told me in September that he found spinners "boring" and preferred his drawing book. By November, he had three spinners and had stopped drawing at break. When I asked him why, he said, "Everyone has them. If I don't play, I sit alone."

I noticed he didn't smile while spinning. He smiled when he drew.

I set up a small drawing corner during Christmas week and invited a few children, including Yusuf. By Friday, Yusuf was drawing again, and showing his work to a new group.

I think he needed to see that there was more than one group to belong to.

Rehana

qa.q: How many spinners did Yusuf have by November?
qa.a: He had three spinners.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf start playing with spinners even though he found them boring?
qa.a: Yusuf felt afraid of being left out and sitting alone, so fitting in with the group mattered more than what he liked.

qa.q: What did Rehana do that helped Yusuf?
qa.a: Rehana set up a drawing corner and invited a few children, which gave Yusuf another group to belong to.

qa.q: How might the children who joined the drawing corner feel?
qa.a: They may have felt happy to find a new activity and new friends, especially if they also weren't keen on spinners.

grounding: A teacher notes a child who changes his taste to match a class craze because being included matters more.
